human_tolerance.notes: Lives in deciduous woodland and urban parks throughout the eastern United States and southern Canada, and turns up in gardens where there is brush, log piles, rocks or shrubs to provide cover. It defends its burrow and darts for cover rather than confronting.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: During the winter the chipmunk may enter long periods of hibernation, modelled here as torpor rather than deep hibernation because it also stores food in its burrow and is active on mild days. The month bounds and temperature thresholds are authored; the article gives no dates or temperatures.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: The first of two breeding seasons runs from February to April.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: The second breeding season runs from June to August; females usually produce one or two litters of three to five young.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Pups stay with their mother for around six to eight weeks, which is the only period besides courtship and mating when chipmunks interact with each other.

vocalizations.description: One of five stereotyped sounds in the chipmunk's repertoire, the chip, a short single note.
A trill measured at up to 130 trills per minute, used in alarm and in defence of the burrow.
The whistle or squeal of the repertoire, a sharp rising note given when an observer or a predator comes close.

taxonomy.note: Sciuridae, Tamias, (Linnaeus, 1758). Linnaeus classified it as Sciurus striatus; Illiger moved it to Tamias in 1811. It is the only living member of the genus.

external.note: GBIF usage key 2437438 and iNaturalist taxon 46217; ITIS TSN 45474 from Wikidata P685.

conservation.note: Found throughout the eastern United States and southern Canada, including urban parks, and with no threat described, consistent with Least Concern; no IUCN page was consulted because those are not openly licensed.

range.note: A chipmunk species found in eastern North America, throughout the eastern United States and southern Canada.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: It climbs trees well and spends most of the day foraging, running along the ground and over logs; it darts away at a gallop when a predator appears. Climb is left out of locomotion_modes because the quadruped body plan has no climb pose to draw.

traits.nest_type.note: Burrow: it constructs underground nests with extensive tunnel systems, often with several entrances, lined with leaves, rocks and sticks.

traits.perching.note: It climbs trees well but forages mainly on the ground and lives in a burrow, so it is not treated as a perching animal.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: about 100 g is over 50 g and under 1 kg, so Small.

traits.mass_kg.note: The article gives a range of 66-150 g and no mean; 100 g is the mid-range value, rounded.

traits.length_m.note: About 30 cm in length including the tail.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Judgement. The article gives total length (about 30 cm including the tail) and body weight but no shoulder height; 7.5 cm is the shoulder height of a small ground squirrel of that length, so treat it as an estimate.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'On average, eastern chipmunks live three or more years in the wild, but in captivity they may live as long as eight years.'

traits.diet.note: 'It prefers bulbs, seeds, fruits, nuts, green plants, mushrooms, insects, worms, and bird eggs', transported in cheek pouches. Mast is the nuts, seed the seeds and bulbs, fruit the berries, browse the green plants, invertebrate the insects and worms, vertebrate the bird eggs.

traits.social.note: 'The eastern chipmunk defends its burrow and lives a solitary life, except during mating season'; members interact only while courting and mating and for the six to eight weeks pups spend with their mother.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The chipmunk is mainly active during the day, spending most of its day foraging.'

traits.defense.note: It defends its burrow and relies on rocky areas, brush or log piles for cover, running for cover when threatened; hawks, owls, foxes, raccoons, snakes, weasels, coyotes, bobcats, lynx, dogs and cats are all listed predators.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement, set from its dependence on cover (rocky areas, brush, log piles, shrubs), its solitary burrow defence and its long list of predators, in a species that does live in urban parks.

habitat.use.note: It can climb trees well, but constructs underground nests and spends most of the day foraging on the ground.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Underground burrows with extensive tunnel systems and several entrances, which it defends.

habitat.resources.note: Seed, mast, fruit and invertebrate tags from the diet paragraph; burrow from the nest, and log_pile and shrub_thicket from the habitat line about rocky areas, brush, log piles and shrubs for cover. Weights are authored to match the diet shares.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'The eastern chipmunk lives in deciduous wooded areas and urban parks throughout the eastern United States and southern Canada. It prefers locations with rocky areas, brush or log piles, and shrubs to provide cover.'

seasonal.strategy.note: 'During the winter, the chipmunk may enter long periods of hibernation.' The record models this as torpor with authored temperature thresholds rather than as full hibernation, because the same article has the animal storing food in its burrow and describes no deep hibernation; the strategy is a judgement between the two options the format offers.

seasonal.triggers.note: Authored. The article mentions winter hibernation but gives no dates or temperatures, so 3 C for ten days to enter and 5 C for three days to exit are chosen as a shallow-winter threshold pair.

seasonal.phases.note: Two breeding seasons, February to April and June to August, with one or two litters of three to five young; pups stay with their mother around six to eight weeks; and long winter hibernation periods.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Pups remain with their mother for around six to eight weeks, taken as 49 days; scale is an authored juvenile size because no sourced figure was found.

vocalizations.chip.note: 'The vocal repertoire of the chipmunk consists of five more or less stereotyped sounds: the chip, the chuck, the trills, the whistle or squeal, and chatter.'

vocalizations.trill.note: The trills of that repertoire, 'measured to occur at the rate of 130 trills per minute'.

vocalizations.squeal.note: The whistle or squeal of the repertoire, described as one of the five stereotyped sounds.

look.note: Reddish-brown fur on the upper body with five dark brown stripes separated by light brown stripes along the back, ending in a dark tail, lighter fur below, a tawny stripe running from the whiskers to below the ears and light stripes over the eyes. Proportions are authored.

behavior.note: The shared ground-forager program fits an animal that spends most of the day foraging on seeds and nuts, drinks and explores near its burrow, rests in cover through the hottest part of the day and bolts for cover when threatened. Parameters are authored: walk to forage, gallop to flee.
